Assessment & Plan (Integrating DDx)

Key findings  
• 48-year-old woman with 6-day history of dysuria, foul-smelling urine, intermittent midline suprapubic pain (7/10), and small visible blood spots in urine.  
• No fever, flank/loin pain, nausea, vomiting, or prior similar episodes.  
• Past history of IBS; taking Mebeverine; allergic to clindamycin.  

Working diagnosis  
• Acute uncomplicated bacterial cystitis – supported by classic lower-tract urinary symptoms without systemic features or flank pain (DDx highest-ranked).  

Management  
• Oral antibiotic for 3 days (prescribed; drug not specified in transcript).  
• Advice: increase oral fluids to 2.5–3 L/day, consider cranberry juice, commercial urinary alkaliniser sachets, purchase thermometer to monitor temperature.  
• Safety-net: seek review if pain worsens, develops back/loin pain, fever, urinary retention, or recurrence.  
• Prescription sent to patient’s nominated pharmacy; expected ready within one hour.  

Considerations (other plausible DDx)  
• Urethritis secondary to STI (medium likelihood) – limited sexual history; reassess if symptoms persist or recur.  
• Distal urinary tract calculi (low–medium likelihood) – hematuria and pain could suggest stone; absence of colicky flank pain makes less likely.

Summary of Differential Diagnoses (from DDx)

1. Acute uncomplicated bacterial cystitis – High likelihood. Acute dysuria with malodorous urine, suprapubic pain, mild hematuria, no systemic or flank features.  
2. Urethritis (Chlamydia/Gonorrhoea) – Medium likelihood. Dysuria ± hematuria possible; limited sexual history; no discharge.  
3. Urinary tract calculi – Low–Medium likelihood. Hematuria and pain could fit, but pain not colicky and no flank radiation.
